title: Feast Calendar
summary: Exodus 23 and Leviticus 23 describe recurring times for Israel’s worship, including weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, and three annual festivals. The instructions connect the calendar with rest, remembrance, harvest, and gathering before God. Other cited texts add distinct settings rather than describing one continuous calendar.
historical_context: Exodus 23 and Leviticus 23 give instructions for festivals, 1 Kings 8 narrates a temple dedication held during a festival in the seventh month, and Hebrews 10 argues about repeated sacrifices and Christ’s offering. These texts provide instructions and later interpretation, not a full record of how every community observed the calendar. This object has no separate source on historical practice in the Second Temple period.
canonical_context: Exodus 23:14–17 names three annual festivals: Unleavened Bread, the harvest festival, and the Festival of Ingathering. Leviticus 23:1–8 begins with the Sabbath and then details Passover and the seven days of Unleavened Bread. In 1 Kings 8:1–66, the temple dedication takes place in the seventh month during a festival, though the passage does not name that festival in the cited verses. Hebrews 10:1–18, by contrast, discusses repeated sacrifices and Christ’s offering; it interprets sacrificial practice but does not explain the feast calendar.
literary_context: The references use distinct forms: Exodus 23 and Leviticus 23 give covenant instruction, 1 Kings 8 narrates a royal temple dedication during a festival, and Hebrews 10 develops an argument about repeated sacrifices and Christ’s offering. Keeping law, narrative, and later argument distinct helps prevent Hebrews from being treated as a calendar list.
covenantal_significance: Exodus 23 links Unleavened Bread with Israel’s departure from Egypt and connects harvest and ingathering with annual worship before God. Leviticus 23 begins with the Sabbath and gives instructions for Passover and Unleavened Bread. The calendar therefore joins rest, remembrance, harvest, and ingathering in Israel’s worship. Hebrews 10 makes a separate argument about sacrifice and Christ; it should not be used to erase the specific meanings of the festivals in these instructions.
canonical_role: Feast Calendar serves as an institutional anchor, connecting social practice, worship, leadership, and covenant life across related passages and themes.

interpretive_notes.note: The feast calendar and the sacrificial system are related but not identical. Exodus 23 and Leviticus 23 give calendar instructions; Hebrews 10 discusses repeated offerings. Read Hebrews’ argument on sacrifice without assuming it restates or replaces every festival practice.

The cited New Testament passage is Hebrews 10, which interprets sacrifice in relation to Christ’s offering. It does not discuss the calendar as a whole. Claims about Christian observance or later Jewish practice would require sources beyond those attached here.
